title: Bram and the Will
premise: True-crime podcaster Tamsin Ravensworth built a career on closing cold cases, but the Ravensworth family's own sealed history has always been off-limits: thirty years ago, their aunt Elspeth drowned in the mill pond and the village of Hollowmere swore it was an accident. When a confession letter arrives postmarked the day after the last witness's funeral, Tamsin returns to Hollowmere to find that everyone who 'moved on' did so by agreeing on a lie. As they peel back the pact, Tamsin discovers their own parents helped bury the truth — and that the confessor is dying and wants absolution before silence wins again. In the end, Tamsin must choose between protecting the family name and broadcasting the truth, closing the case at last but severing themselves from everything they thought belonging meant.
about_author: Mara Yarrow grew up in a river town where everyone knew which families kept secrets and which kept ledgers. A former archivist turned novelist, she writes mysteries about small places that remember too much.

chapters.title: Postmarked Yesterday
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. On the eve of launching a new season, Tamsin receives a handwritten confession to a drowning thirty years old — postmarked the day after the sender's own funeral was announced. The beat: professional curiosity curdling into personal dread as they recognize the handwriting.

chapters.title: The Case I Swore Off
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Flashback-tinged chapter establishing the rule: never cover the Ravensworth case. Their mother calls, warning them off in one sentence. Emotional beat: the first crack in Tamsin's belief that they chose this career freely.

chapters.title: Hollowmere in Winter
chapters.summary: Tamsin arrives; alternating close-third from villager Nell Ashcombe, who watches the outsider step off the bus. The mill pond is frozen over, the town shuttered and watchful. Beat: the uncanny feeling of being recognized by people you don't recognize.

chapters.title: A Funeral Already Held
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. They visit the grave of the letter's supposed author, Harold Vane, dead two weeks — yet the letter references events only he could know. Beat: grief for a man they never met, and the vertigo of a mystery with no living suspect.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Kept
chapters.summary: Nell's POV. Nell, the parish records keeper, shows Tamsin a ledger page torn out the week after Elspeth died. She helps reluctantly, bound by her own promise. Beat: loyalty shown as quiet sabotage of one's own conscience.

chapters.title: Three Who Stayed
chapters.summary: Tamsin interviews the three surviving witnesses: the doctor, the ferryman, and their own father's old friend. Each tells the same story with identical phrasing. Beat: the horror of rehearsed memory.

chapters.title: My Mother's Silence
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, phone call chapter. Confronting their mother yields only 'some things keep a family alive.' Tamsin realizes the podcaster's creed — truth above all — was inherited from someone who broke it. Beat: betrayal at the root of identity.

chapters.title: The Pond Under Ice
chapters.summary: Nell's POV. Nell takes Tamsin to the mill at night and reveals she saw something that night as a child but was made to forget. Beat: fear of what remembering will cost her standing in the only home she's known.

chapters.title: Harold's Last Season
chapters.summary: Tamsin finds Harold Vane's rented room, untouched since his death: newspaper clippings, a second draft of the confession, and a list of names — including Tamsin's parents. Beat: the confessor becomes a character, pitiable and deliberate.

chapters.title: An Accident, Repeatedly
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Reconstructing the official record, they find the coroner's report contradicts itself across three copies. Someone with authority edited the file. Beat: the machinery of respectability exposed as complicity.

chapters.title: The Ferryman Breaks
chapters.summary: Ferryman's POV. Old Cobb, drunk and terrified, admits he pulled Elspeth from the water alive — and that someone paid him to say otherwise. He won't say who. Beat: survival's price named aloud for the first time.

chapters.title: Threats, Politely Worded
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. An anonymous note offers to fund the podcast generously if the season changes subject. Then Nell is followed home. Beat: menace arriving not as violence but as civility, which is worse.

chapters.title: Elspeth, Alive in the Record
chapters.summary: Nell's POV. Digging into diaries and letters, the pair discover Elspeth was planning to leave Hollowmere — and knew a secret about the town's most respected family. Beat: the victim reassembled from erasure, becoming a person rather than a plot point.

chapters.title: My Father's Name on the List
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The list confirms their father handled the money that bought the witnesses' silence. Tamsin confronts the possibility that their entire childhood was funded by a cover-up. Beat: shame and fury braided together.

chapters.title: The Second Confession
chapters.summary: Tamsin finds a draft addressed not to police but to Elspeth's daughter, never sent. It names no killer — only says 'we let the water decide and called it God.' Beat: moral ambiguity deepening; guilt without a villain.

chapters.title: Someone Else Knows
chapters.summary: Nell's POV. Nell realizes the threats match phrases from the torn ledger page — meaning whoever is watching read it recently. The watcher isn't one of the three witnesses. Beat: paranoia; the past has an active agent in the present.

chapters.title: The Mill at Thaw
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Lured to the mill by a note signed 'E,' Tamsin is nearly hurt when the ice gives way — staged or accidental, unclear. Beat: terror, and the realization the danger is now physical and immediate.

chapters.title: The Doctor's Ledger
chapters.summary: Doctor's POV, deathbed scene. The last signatory confesses: Elspeth discovered the family's fraud that kept half the village in debt, and the 'accident' was arranged by the man everyone revered. Beat: relief and revulsion — truth obtained at the cost of a dying man's dignity.

chapters.title: What Belonging Costs
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Armed with proof, Tamsin faces the choice: air the episode and destroy their parents' legacy, or bury it like everyone else. Their mother finally asks them to bury it. Beat: the theme crystallized — loyalty versus truth, with no clean side.

chapters.title: Broadcast
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, climax. Tamsin airs the full season: the fraud, the drowning, the pact, their own family's role, naming themselves among the guilty. The town erupts; some thank them, some never will. Beat: catharsis laced with loss.

chapters.title: After the Water Decides
chapters.summary: Nell's POV. Weeks later: the mill pond unfrozen, the town raw but breathing, some reckonings begun. Nell chooses to stay and rebuild; she and Tamsin part as friends. Beat: quiet hope — survival can mean change, not just endurance.

chapters.title: The Case I Closed
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, coda. Recording the final episode alone, Tamsin revises their creed: some cases close you before you close them. They leave the door open for Elspeth's daughter's call. Beat: bittersweet resolution — belonging redefined as honesty, even when it costs everything else.
